questions.q: In the opening example, Tunde was charged for Ada's rice although every type was correct. What was the real bug?
questions.explain: Types describe shapes, not how long objects live or who shares them. The cart was correct as a type and wrong as a lifetime. Scopes give each request its own instance.
options: A missing type annotation on Cart
A lifetime bug: one Cart was created at startup and shared by every request, although a cart must live for one request only
A race condition between two async functions
The cart's items array should have been readonly

questions.q: What is the composition root?
questions.explain: Services only declare what they need in their constructors. The composition root (hand-written or a container) is the only code that knows the concrete classes and how they fit together.
options: The base class all services extend
The one place, usually the program's entry point, where the object graph is wired: dependencies are created and passed to the services that need them
The folder that contains the node_modules
The first service a container resolves

questions.q: Why can't container.resolve(Clock) work when Clock is an interface?
questions.explain: TypeScript reports "'Clock' only refers to a type, but is being used as a value here." A container needs a key that exists at runtime: a string, a symbol, a class or a token object.
options: Because interfaces cannot have methods
Interfaces are erased at compile time, so there is no runtime value to use as a key
Because resolve only accepts strings
It works if the interface is exported

questions.q: What is wrong with using plain strings such as "clock" as tokens?
questions.explain: The string exists at runtime but says nothing about the type registered under it. A token object carries its type (through a phantom type parameter) and is unique by identity.
options: Strings are slower to compare than objects
A string carries no type, so resolve<Clock>("clock") is a claim, and two modules can accidentally use the same string
Maps cannot use strings as keys
Strings cannot be exported

questions.q: What does declare readonly __type: T do in class Token<T>?
questions.explain: Without a property that uses T, every Token<X> has the same shape and TypeScript could not tell them apart. The declare field exists only for the type checker.
options: It stores the registered value on the token
It checks at runtime that the resolved value has type T
It emits no JavaScript, but makes Token<Clock> and Token<Logger> structurally different, so resolve can infer the right type
It makes the token immutable

questions.q: A file creates new Token<Clock>("Clock") instead of importing the exported CLOCK. What happens when it resolves it?
questions.explain: Token identity is the key; the name is only for messages. The type is identical, so the compiler cannot help. Export each token from exactly one module and import it everywhere.
options: It gets the registered clock, because the name matches
A compile error, because the types differ
A runtime "nothing registered" error: the new token is a different object, so a different key
It gets undefined with no error

questions.q: Why is register declared with <T, const D extends readonly Token<unknown>[]>?
questions.explain: Without const, [CART, CLOCK] would be inferred as an array of a union, and TypesOf could not map position 0 to Cart and position 1 to Clock.
options: const makes the dependency list immutable at runtime
const makes TypeScript infer [CART, CLOCK] as a tuple, so each position keeps its own token type and the factory's parameters can be checked in order
It prevents the same token being registered twice
const type parameters are required for classes

questions.q: What is TypesOf<[Token<Cart>, Token<Clock>, Token<Logger>]>?
questions.explain: A mapped type over a tuple maps each position separately. The conditional type with infer U pulls the type out of each token, keeping the order, so the result can be a factory's parameter list.
options: (Cart | Clock | Logger)[]
[Cart, Clock, Logger]
Token<Cart | Clock | Logger>
[Token<Cart>, Token<Clock>, Token<Logger>]

questions.q: The lesson's registerClass(token, lifetime, deps, type) types type as new (...deps: TypesOf<D>) => T. Which mistake does that catch?
questions.explain: The constructor's real parameter list is compared with the types of the tokens, position by position. Whether those tokens are registered, and with which lifetime, is runtime information.
options: A dependency that was never registered
A cycle between two classes
Dependency tokens in the wrong order, too few of them, or of the wrong type for the constructor
A scoped dependency held by a singleton

questions.q: Which lifetime fits a shopping cart that belongs to one HTTP request?
questions.explain: Scoped means one instance per scope, and a web server creates one scope per request. Every service in that request shares the cart; the next request gets a new one.
options: Singleton
Scoped
Transient
Any; lifetimes only affect performance

questions.q: Which lifetime fits a database connection pool?
questions.explain: A pool exists precisely to share a few connections across all requests. Creating one per request (or per resolve) would open connections until the database refused them.
options: Singleton: it is expensive to create and designed to be shared by the whole process
Scoped: one pool per request
Transient: a new pool every time a repository needs one
It should not be in the container

questions.q: Why must a container refuse a singleton that depends on a scoped service?
questions.explain: This is a captive dependency: a longer-lived object captures a shorter-lived one. With a scoped cart or current user it becomes a data leak between customers.
options: Because singletons cannot have dependencies
The singleton is built once and would keep the first request's instance forever, handing it to every later request
Because scoped services are slower
It should not; this is a normal pattern

questions.q: DailyReport (singleton) needs CheckoutService (transient), which needs Cart (scoped). Is Cart captive?
questions.explain: What matters is the longest-lived object above the scoped one on the path. That is why the lesson's container looks for any singleton on the path, not only the direct parent.
options: No: a transient in between breaks the chain
Yes: the transient checkout is built once, for the singleton, so it and its cart live as long as the singleton
Only if the report is resolved at the root
No: transient services cannot depend on scoped ones

questions.q: How does the lesson's #resolve detect a cycle such as OrderService -> InvoiceService -> OrderService?
questions.explain: Resolving is a depth-first walk of the dependency graph. A token that appears twice on the current path is a cycle; naive recursion would instead overflow the stack. The path also makes the error message useful.
options: By counting how many instances were created
With a timeout
It passes the path of tokens being resolved down the recursion, and fails when the current token is already on the path
TypeScript reports it at compile time

questions.q: Why is "nothing is registered for PaymentGateway" not a compile error in an ordinary container?
questions.explain: Which registrations ran can depend on conditions, loops or plugins. Only a design whose type changes with each registration (the lesson's builder) can move this error to compile time.
options: Because TypeScript does not check method calls
Registration happens through runtime calls; the container's type is the same before and after each register, so the compiler cannot know which tokens were registered
Because tokens are symbols
It is a compile error if strict is on

questions.q: A factory lists FIXED_CLOCK where SYSTEM_CLOCK was meant; both are Token<Clock>. What catches it?
questions.explain: Types compare shapes. Two tokens of the same type are interchangeable to the compiler, and the container happily resolves whichever you asked for. Give such tokens very different names and test the composition root.
options: The compiler, because the token names differ
The container, because it checks names at runtime
Nothing automatic: both tokens have the same type, so only review or a test of the real wiring can catch it
The const type parameter

questions.q: What is the best practical defence against the wiring errors types cannot catch?
questions.explain: A missing registration, a cycle or a captive dependency found at startup stops the deployment. Found at the first request, it stops a customer.
options: Adding more type annotations to services
Catching errors around every resolve call
Validating the container at startup (resolve every top-level service or check the graph) and testing the real composition root
Making every service a singleton

questions.q: The typed ServiceBuilder makes a missing service a compile error. What does it cost?
questions.explain: The builder's type grows with each add, so it must see every registration in one place and in dependency order. That fits small apps and libraries; frameworks with modules usually prefer a runtime container plus startup checks.
options: Nothing; it is strictly better than a runtime container
Registration order is fixed by the dependencies, everything is one chained expression, plugins cannot add services at runtime, and scopes need extra machinery
Services can no longer be tested with fakes
It only works with classes

questions.q: In add<K extends string, T>(name: K extends keyof S ? never : K, …), what does K extends keyof S ? never : K achieve?
questions.explain: No string is assignable to never, so a duplicate name is refused with "not assignable to parameter of type 'never'". It is a conditional type used as a guard.
options: It makes names case-insensitive
A name that is already a service becomes never, so adding it twice is a compile error
It removes the service from the builder
It allows only one service in total

questions.q: In @zudojs/container, what lifetime does registerFactory(token, factory) use when you pass no scope?
questions.explain: The package defaults to ContainerScope.TRANSIENT. registerValue is always a singleton, because a value provider returns the same object anyway. Many other containers default to singleton, so check before you rely on sharing.
options: Singleton
Scoped
Transient: a new instance on every resolve
It throws until you choose one

questions.q: container.registerClass(CHECKOUT, CheckoutService, { inject: [CLOCK, CART, LOGGER] }) has the first two tokens swapped. What happens with @zudojs/container?
questions.explain: registerFactory types the factory's parameters from its inject list; registerClass does not check inject against the constructor. A one-line factory, (cart, clock, log) => new CheckoutService(cart, clock, log), makes the mistake a compile error.
options: A compile error, like registerFactory
It compiles, because the class is typed as Constructor<T> with any[] parameters, and fails later at runtime inside the service
The container reorders the tokens by type
A CircularDependencyError

questions.q: Why should services receive dependencies through their constructors instead of calling container.resolve themselves?
questions.explain: Calling the container from inside services is the "service locator" style. Constructor parameters make dependencies explicit and typed, so a test can pass fakes directly and the composition root shows the whole graph.
options: Because resolve is slow
A service that pulls from the container hides what it needs, cannot be built without the container, and its wiring cannot be checked or seen in one place
Because constructors run before the container exists
There is no difference

questions.q: A small service has eight classes and no per-request state. Should it use a DI container?
questions.explain: Dependency injection is the idea (pass dependencies in); a container is a tool for doing the wiring. Fakes work just as well with hand wiring, as the Classes lesson showed.
options: Yes, every TypeScript project needs one
Probably not: hand wiring in one composition root is clearer; a container pays off when lifetimes, scopes and many services make hand wiring error-prone
Yes, otherwise it cannot be tested
No, containers do not work with classes

questions.q: Finish resolve: return the cached instance if there is one; otherwise look up the factory (throw Error("nothing registered for NAME") if there is none), build the instance, cache it and return it. The program should print the three lines shown.
questions.explain: The token's phantom type makes resolve(DB) return the pool type, so query is checked. The two casts are safe because a value is only ever stored under the token it was built for.

pool 1: SELECT 1
true 1
Error: nothing registered for Mailer

questions.q: Make resolve detect cycles: pass the path of names being resolved down the recursion and throw Error("circular dependency: A -> B -> A") when a name is already on it. The program should print Clock() and the cycle.
questions.explain: The path is exactly the chain of "needs" that led here, so the same array detects the cycle and explains it. Checking before looking up the registration means the error names the cycle, not a later symptom.
questions.expected:
Clock()
Error: circular dependency: OrderService -> InvoiceService -> TaxService -> OrderService

questions.q: Finish createScope: the returned resolver caches singletons in the container's shared map and scoped instances in a map that belongs to that scope only. The program should print the three lines shown.
questions.explain: Each call to createScope creates a new scoped map, captured by the returned closure, so each request has its own cart. Singletons go to the one map owned by the container, so every scope shares the configuration.

questions.q: Write checkCaptive(path): when the last name on the path is scoped and any earlier name is a singleton, return "captive: HOLDER would keep TARGET"; otherwise return "ok". The program should print the three lines shown.
questions.explain: Looking only at the direct parent would miss the first case: the transient checkout in the middle is built once for the singleton report, so the cart would live forever too. A singleton depending on another singleton is fine.
questions.expected:
captive: DailyReport would keep Cart
ok
ok

questions.q: Write resolveAll(tokens). It returns the registered values as a tuple typed per token (use the given TypesOf and a const type parameter), and throws Error("nothing registered for NAME") for a missing one. The program should print NGN 30000.00 and the error.
questions.explain: With const D the argument stays a tuple, and TypesOf<D> gives [string, number], so the starter's as [string, number] is no longer needed and a swapped destructuring would be a type error. The cast inside is safe because map keeps one value per token, in order.

Error: nothing registered for FeatureFlag

questions.q: Register the three services in @zudojs/container: the clock as a value, the cart as a scoped factory, and the checkout with registerFactory so its dependencies are type-checked. The program should print 2 item(s) on 2026-09-24 for the first request and 0 item(s) on 2026-09-24 for a new one.
questions.explain: The factory's cart and clock parameters are typed from [CART, CLOCK], so swapping the tokens would not compile. The checkout is transient (the default), so each request builds one around its own scoped cart.

questions.q: Write missingDependencies(graph): for every service, list each dependency that is not itself a key of the graph, as "SERVICE needs DEP". The program should print the two missing dependencies.
questions.explain: This is the cheapest startup check a container can run: it reads registrations only and builds nothing, so it cannot trigger side effects. It turns the error types cannot catch into a failed deployment instead of a failed request.
questions.expected:
CheckoutService needs Logger
ReceiptPrinter needs PaymentGateway
